title: Rin's River Message
markdown:
Rain tapped Rin’s burrow window. Rin was a river seal, fur dark as a moonless night, eyes with a sparkle of distant stars. She loved her river: familiar currents, the gurgle of fresh water, clear and cool and tasting of home. When sun broke the clouds it dappled the bed. Reeds whispered. Today the raindrops seemed to talk of far oceans, the kind in her worn books — explorers, stormy captains, treasures. Her own life felt rather sealed. Voyages were for pages. Her world was gentle flow and known faces.

She pressed her nose to the glass until it misted. The stack of books by her bed had salt-stained maps and captains who never needed to dry their flippers. One map showed a sea like a blue plate. Another showed a storm the illustrator had drawn with too much ink. She had read one chapter twice that morning and still felt no closer to a voyage of her own.

A flash of white and a boisterous squawk: Puck the paperboy gull, wings ruffled from delivering news, beady eyes missing nothing. A feathered newspaper.

“Glorious day for it,” he cawed, landing and scattering droplets. “Damp isn’t ideal for paperboys. Message for Mrs. Higgins about her prize petunias, but the ink’s running. You’d think they’d invent waterproof ink for important petunia announcements.”

A gentle thump on the glass. Bobbing in the weeds, a small bottle, corked, faded red ribbon, a tiny scroll inside. It had come downriver and parked at her window. Rin’s heart fluttered. Whiskers twitched.

Adventure — and then a frown. Message bottles belonged in the salty sea, in books, not in her fresh familiar river. What if it was meant for someone else?

“What are you waiting for?” Puck nudged. “Mystery. My fish and bread.”

“It’s a message in a bottle. In the river. It isn’t supposed to be here.”

“The river leads to the sea. The sea leads to exciting things. Adventure awaits, even if it’s damp.”

She turned the bottle without pulling the cork. The scroll looked impossibly thin. Opening it here, in her own weeds, felt like reading someone else’s diary. Puck hopped from sill to weed-tip and back, leaving wet prints like commas. “If it wanted to stay a secret,” he said, “it should have picked a less nosy window.” She set the bottle back in the current instead, as if the river might know the address.

She slipped into the cool water, determined and nervous. The bottle drifted. Puck circled. “Hold on, little bottle.”

The chase unfolded the known river into something urgent. Rin swam a dark torpedo, dodging submerged branches and grey stones. Puck swooped, trying to steer with his beak; the bottle bobbed with a will of its own. Sleepy turtles on mossy logs. Minnows scattering like silver confetti. They passed the willow where Rin usually napped, and the bend where the current always pulled left, and a sunken rowboat she had never bothered to inspect. A turtle opened one eye and shut it again, as if bottles were not news. Minnows made a silver burst and came back together. Today every familiar thing asked to be noticed.

Farther on, the river widened. Banks went vague. A forgotten fishing net hung like a ghostly hammock. “Whoa.” Puck nearly tangled. Rin twisted through the ropes, felt one catch her shoulder, wriggled free. Puck flapped the bottle clear, then had to flap himself clear when a loop tried for his tail. Rin shoved the mesh with her shoulder until it sagged enough to let a gull through. An unusual team, and a good one.

The water changed: heavier, more buoyant. Rin felt it in her flippers. A kick that used to sink her a little now held her up. Puck, who flew the estuary to seaside cottages, landed on a floating branch. “You’re sitting higher. The bottle too, like it’s wearing a little hat.”

“It feels thicker.”

“River meets sea,” Puck said, proud of facts picked up on rounds. “Salt water is denser than fresh. Things float a bit higher. More buoyant.” He hopped the branch to show how little it dipped.

The tastes mixed: home-water and a clean bite of salt. Reeds gave way to piles and rust. The bottle sat up straighter, ribbon dark with wet. Rin tried floating still, flippers folded, and found the water held her as if it had grown a little prouder. Puck pecked the bottle’s cork and it barely ducked.

Seaside Dock bustled: tall ships, masts like bare trees, gulls who thought they owned the waterfront, brine and fish and tar. The bottle nudged a barnacled pier. Rin clambered out, shaking, bottle in her paws. Puck scanned crates, coils of rope, a crate of lemons going sour, and a chalkboard of sailings that the rain had already begun to eat.

“Right then, Captain Barnacle?” he asked the air.

No Captain Barnacle. Bustle, fish-smell, arguing gulls. A grumpy pelican waddled over, beak like a scoop. “What’s all this? Lost trinkets cluttering prime real estate.”

“We’re looking for Captain Barnacle,” Rin said, holding up the faded ribbon. “This message is for him.”

The pelican scoffed. “Never heard of him. Myth, like a mermaid’s comb. Scurry off. Sunbathing spot.”

Rin almost asked if he would at least look at the ribbon. He had already turned, claiming a warm plank with the dignity of a king who had never heard of captains. Puck muttered a headline under his breath — LOCAL PELICAN UNHELPFUL — and scanned the masts anyway, in case a Barnacle had simply forgotten to answer to his name.

The moody grey sky opened. Wind howled. Sea went froth. Rain hammered. A dark wave surged over the pier and snatched the bottle from Rin’s paws. Tossed, tumbled, gone.

A hollow ache. The mystery swallowed. Maybe she should have stayed home. Books felt flimsy. She stared at the place the ribbon had been and saw only foam.

Puck’s cheer dampened. “I’m so sorry.”

She had never even read the words.

They crouched in the lee of a crate while the worst of the wind tried the pilings. Puck’s feathers stuck in unhappy points. Rin thought of Mrs. Higgins’s running ink and of every page she had ever trusted to stay put. A coil of rope slapped the dock. Somewhere a hatch banged. The first bottle did not come back.

Then Puck’s head tilted, eyes sharp. Near a fishing boat hunkered in the storm: another bottle, another faded red ribbon, caught in a small eddy.

Curiosity pushed through. Rin made her way along the slippery pier, flippers finding wet wood, past the crate and the sour lemons, and nudged the second bottle closer. Smaller. The cork was newer. Not a scroll — a child’s wobbly drawing of a river seal who looked remarkably like her, and a note in bright letters: To my friend Rin, who lives by the river.

A friend. By the river. Puck grinned wide.

The first bottle, lost to the sea, had not been for this Rin. It had been for another Rin, perhaps one who knew a Captain Barnacle. This second bottle was hers.

Warmth better than any sunbeam. Not a pirate map. A message from a child, meant for the seal at the river window. The drawn seal had a slightly too-round nose and a grin that did not care about captains. Rin held the glass so the rain would not smudge the bright letters.

Rain softened to a patter. They did not open the lost bottle, because it was gone; they did not need to. Rin carried her bottle home against the current, which was harder work and somehow better. At the willow she paused so the drawing could stay upright. At the stepping-stones of the riverbed she knew by heart she did not look for captains. Puck produced a slightly damp biscuit. “Celebratory snack.”

She settled by the glass, the happy drawn seal beside her, river sounding like a contented sigh. The rain kept tapping. Puck preened ink-speckled feathers and grumbled, almost fondly, that petunia news would have to wait until the ink dried. The petunias, somewhere upstream, would get their news tomorrow, waterproof or not.
characters: Rin (a river seal), Puck (a paperboy gull)
